name: Repetition
definition: One completed performance of an exercise movement using the agreed start and finish positions. The counting convention should stay consistent across sessions.
example: Eight complete presses are eight repetitions.
caution: A partial repetition and a full-range repetition are different tasks even when both are counted as one.

diagram.title: Repetition
diagram.caption: Eight complete presses are eight repetitions.

name: Set
definition: A group of repetitions performed together before a rest or a change of exercise. A set is a container for work, not a fixed amount of training stimulus.
example: Three sets of eight means three separate groups of eight repetitions.
caution: Twenty easy repetitions and five demanding repetitions can both be one set.

diagram.title: Set
diagram.caption: Three sets of eight means three separate groups of eight repetitions.

name: Working set
definition: A set intended to provide the main training work rather than only prepare for it. The distinction depends on the session plan, not a universal weight cutoff.
example: Two lighter practice sets precede three planned working sets.
caution: A very demanding warm-up can still add fatigue even if you exclude it from the working-set total.

diagram.title: Working set
diagram.caption: Two lighter practice sets precede three planned working sets.

name: Warm-up set
definition: A preparatory set used to rehearse an exercise and approach the planned working load. It can also reveal whether the setup or planned demand needs adjustment.
example: An easy machine-press set lets you check the seat position before adding weight.
caution: Warm-up sets do not need to become a second workout.

diagram.title: Warm-up set
diagram.caption: An easy machine-press set lets you check the seat position before adding weight.

name: Load
definition: The resistance used for an exercise. In a log this often means external mass, but bands, bodyweight, leverage, and machines make the mechanical task more complicated.
example: A dumbbell press may be logged as 16 kg per hand.
caution: Do not compare two cable stacks as if identical printed weights necessarily mean identical resistance.

diagram.title: Load
diagram.caption: A dumbbell press may be logged as 16 kg per hand.

name: 1RM
definition: One-repetition maximum: the greatest load a person can lift once for a specified exercise and movement standard under the test conditions.
example: A tested bench-press 1RM applies to that bench-press standard.
caution: It is exercise-specific and can change with technique, fatigue, and testing conditions. Testing is not necessary for every training plan.
aliases: one rep max one repetition maximum

diagram.title: 1RM
diagram.caption: A tested bench-press 1RM applies to that bench-press standard.

name: Estimated 1RM
definition: A prediction of one-repetition maximum calculated from another performance, such as a submaximal set. The formula and closeness to failure affect the estimate.
example: A calculator uses load and repetitions to estimate a maximum without a maximal attempt.
caution: A calculated personal record is not the same as actually lifting that load. Estimates from high-repetition sets can be especially uncertain.

diagram.title: Estimated 1RM
diagram.caption: A calculator uses load and repetitions to estimate a maximum without a maximal attempt.

name: RIR
definition: Repetitions in reserve: your estimate of additional repetitions possible before the specified endpoint of the set. It is a subjective estimate.
example: About 2 RIR means you believe roughly two more comparable repetitions were available.
caution: Accuracy varies. Discomfort and technique changes can alter what you mean by another possible repetition.
aliases: reps in reserve repetitions in reserve

diagram.title: RIR
diagram.caption: About 2 RIR means you believe roughly two more comparable repetitions were available.

name: RPE
definition: Rating of perceived exertion. It reports subjective effort on a named scale. Strength RPE based on RIR and general aerobic exertion scales are not interchangeable.
example: In a common lifting convention, RPE 8 corresponds to roughly 2 RIR.
caution: Always identify the scale. A cardio effort of 8/10 does not imply two repetitions remain.

diagram.title: RPE
diagram.caption: In a common lifting convention, RPE 8 corresponds to roughly 2 RIR.

name: Technical failure
definition: The point at which another repetition cannot be performed within the technique standard you chose. It can occur before you are unable to move the load at all.
example: You stop a row because you can no longer keep the torso position consistent.
caution: Different people may use different technique standards. State yours when comparing sets.

diagram.title: Technical failure
diagram.caption: You stop a row because you can no longer keep the torso position consistent.

name: Momentary muscular failure
definition: In common research usage, the point where the concentric phase cannot be completed despite attempting it under the stated exercise conditions.
example: You attempt another repetition but cannot complete the lifting phase.
caution: It differs from voluntarily stopping because a set feels difficult. Definitions and testing procedures vary between studies.

diagram.title: Momentary muscular failure
diagram.caption: You attempt another repetition but cannot complete the lifting phase.

name: Progressive overload
definition: A principle of increasing or adapting training demand over time as capacity changes. It can involve load, repetitions, sets, range, or another task-relevant variable.
example: You build repetitions at one load before testing the next available load.
caution: It does not require adding weight every workout. Changes should remain interpretable and manageable.

diagram.title: Progressive overload
diagram.caption: You build repetitions at one load before testing the next available load.

name: Double progression
definition: A programming method that progresses repetitions within a chosen range and then increases load when a defined criterion is met.
example: Work from 8 toward 12 reps, then increase load after meeting your rule.
caution: There are several versions. Specify whether the rule applies to every set or another measure.

diagram.title: Double progression
diagram.caption: Work from 8 toward 12 reps, then increase load after meeting your rule.

name: Volume
definition: The amount of training work, expressed using a defined measure such as working sets, repetitions, time, or distance. The unit matters.
example: Six working sets across two weekly sessions is a set-based volume measure.
caution: The word alone does not tell you whether someone means sets, repetitions, or total external weight moved.

diagram.title: Volume
diagram.caption: Six working sets across two weekly sessions is a set-based volume measure.

name: Volume load
definition: The sum of repetitions multiplied by external load across the sets being counted. It is a bookkeeping measure that does not fully capture training stimulus.
example: 3 × 10 × 40 kg equals 1,200 kg of volume load.
caution: Totals across different exercises, ranges, and machines are not directly equivalent.

diagram.title: Volume load
diagram.caption: 3 × 10 × 40 kg equals 1,200 kg of volume load.

name: Frequency
definition: How often a defined activity occurs during a period. It may describe sessions, exercise exposures, or how often a muscle group is trained.
example: Three gym visits is three sessions per week, even if a particular exercise appears only twice.
caution: Session frequency and per-muscle frequency are different measures.

diagram.title: Frequency
diagram.caption: Three gym visits is three sessions per week, even if a particular exercise appears only twice.

name: Hypertrophy
definition: An increase in muscle size. It is different from an immediate pump, short-term swelling, or a change in scale weight alone.
example: Repeated resistance training can produce increases in muscle size over time.
caution: A larger volume-load total does not directly measure hypertrophy.

diagram.title: Hypertrophy
diagram.caption: Repeated resistance training can produce increases in muscle size over time.

name: Strength
definition: The ability to produce force under specified conditions. In a gym it is often assessed by performance on a particular movement and loading task.
example: Improved bench-press performance describes strength in that tested task.
caution: Skill, setup, and movement standard influence test results. Strength is not one universal number.

diagram.title: Strength
diagram.caption: Improved bench-press performance describes strength in that tested task.

name: Power
definition: The rate of doing mechanical work. It relates to force and movement velocity, so producing force quickly matters.
example: Moving a load faster at a given force changes mechanical power.
caution: A heavier but much slower repetition is not automatically a more powerful one.

diagram.title: Power
diagram.caption: Moving a load faster at a given force changes mechanical power.

name: Muscular endurance
definition: The ability to sustain or repeat muscular work over a task. The outcome depends on the exercise, resistance, duration, and test rules.
example: The number of valid repetitions at a fixed load can be one endurance measure.
caution: It is not identical to maximal strength or cardiorespiratory endurance.

diagram.title: Muscular endurance
diagram.caption: The number of valid repetitions at a fixed load can be one endurance measure.

name: Compound exercise
definition: An exercise involving movement at more than one joint. The term describes movement organization, not automatic superiority over other exercises.
example: A squat involves motion at the hips, knees, and ankles.
caution: Muscle contribution depends on technique, range, load, and anatomy.

diagram.title: Compound exercise
diagram.caption: A squat involves motion at the hips, knees, and ankles.

name: Isolation exercise
definition: An exercise emphasizing movement at one joint, often used to focus work on a smaller set of muscles. Other muscles may still stabilize the task.
example: A knee-extension machine primarily trains a knee-extension action.
caution: “Isolation” does not mean only one muscle is active.

diagram.title: Isolation exercise
diagram.caption: A knee-extension machine primarily trains a knee-extension action.

name: Unilateral exercise
definition: An exercise performed with one side at a time or with a deliberately asymmetric emphasis. Log sides clearly.
example: Ten lunges per side is different from ten alternating lunges in total.
caution: Do not silently switch between per-side and total-repetition conventions.

diagram.title: Unilateral exercise
diagram.caption: Ten lunges per side is different from ten alternating lunges in total.

name: Bilateral exercise
definition: An exercise performed with both sides acting together in the main movement. The label does not imply perfectly equal contribution from each side.
example: A conventional two-leg squat is a bilateral exercise.
caution: The total external load is not necessarily divided equally between limbs.

diagram.title: Bilateral exercise
diagram.caption: A conventional two-leg squat is a bilateral exercise.

name: Concentric
definition: A muscle action in which the active muscle shortens while producing force. In many lifts it corresponds to the lifting phase.
example: The elbow flexors shorten during the upward phase of a curl.
caution: “Up” is not a universal definition for every muscle or exercise.

diagram.title: Concentric
diagram.caption: The elbow flexors shorten during the upward phase of a curl.

name: Eccentric
definition: A muscle action in which the active muscle lengthens while producing force. It often controls the lowering phase of a lift.
example: The elbow flexors lengthen while controlling the lowering of a curl.
caution: It is active control, not simply letting a weight fall.

diagram.title: Eccentric
diagram.caption: The elbow flexors lengthen while controlling the lowering of a curl.

name: Isometric
definition: A muscle action producing force without a meaningful change in the joint position being held. Internal muscle and tendon behavior can still be complex.
example: Holding a fixed position against resistance is an isometric task.
caution: A still-looking body does not mean no muscular effort is occurring.

diagram.title: Isometric
diagram.caption: Holding a fixed position against resistance is an isometric task.

name: Range of motion
definition: The movement excursion used at a joint or in an exercise. It can be described with angles or repeatable practical landmarks.
example: A row recorded from full arm reach to a specified handle endpoint has a defined range.
caution: The useful range depends on the task and person; a diagram cannot set an individual pain-free limit.

diagram.title: Range of motion
diagram.caption: A row recorded from full arm reach to a specified handle endpoint has a defined range.

name: Partial repetition
definition: A repetition intentionally or unintentionally using only part of a defined movement range. Which part is trained matters.
example: A partial rep might use the lower half or upper half of an exercise.
caution: Do not assume every partial range has the same effect or compare it silently with full-range work.

diagram.title: Partial repetition
diagram.caption: A partial rep might use the lower half or upper half of an exercise.

name: Tempo
definition: The timing of phases within a repetition, often written as a sequence for lowering, pauses, and lifting. The order should be explained.
example: A note of “3-second lowering” is clearer than an unexplained four-digit code.
caution: The same total repetition time can be distributed across phases in different ways.

diagram.title: Tempo
diagram.caption: A note of “3-second lowering” is clearer than an unexplained four-digit code.

name: Rest interval
definition: The time between defined bouts of work, most commonly between sets. State where timing begins and ends.
example: Two minutes from finishing one set to starting the next is a two-minute inter-set rest.
caution: Rest between exercises and rest between repetitions are different quantities.

diagram.title: Rest interval
diagram.caption: Two minutes from finishing one set to starting the next is a two-minute inter-set rest.

name: Superset
definition: Two exercises performed in sequence with little or no planned rest between them, followed by the specified recovery. Arrangements vary.
example: A press followed by a row can be one superset pairing.
caution: Pairing does not make the exercises physiologically independent; fatigue can carry across.

diagram.title: Superset
diagram.caption: A press followed by a row can be one superset pairing.

name: Autoregulation
definition: Adjusting a training prescription using current performance or feedback instead of relying only on a fixed plan. The decision rule should be explicit.
example: Reduce the load if the warm-up and first set are substantially harder than the planned effort.
caution: It does not mean changing the whole session based on one vague mood or device score.

diagram.title: Autoregulation
diagram.caption: Reduce the load if the warm-up and first set are substantially harder than the planned effort.

name: Specificity
definition: The principle that adaptations and performance improvements relate to the tasks and demands practiced. Transfer between tasks is not unlimited.
example: Practice on one exercise may improve its performance more than an unrelated movement.
caution: Specificity does not mean variation is useless; it means the comparison should match the goal.

diagram.title: Specificity
diagram.caption: Practice on one exercise may improve its performance more than an unrelated movement.

name: Plateau
definition: A period without clear improvement in a chosen outcome across comparable observations. The observation window and measurement error matter.
example: Several comparable sessions show no change in repetitions at a fixed load.
caution: One difficult session does not establish a plateau.

diagram.title: Plateau
diagram.caption: Several comparable sessions show no change in repetitions at a fixed load.

name: Aerobic exercise
definition: Activity that substantially uses aerobic energy production and challenges cardiorespiratory function over time. Energy systems overlap rather than switching completely on or off.
example: Brisk walking or sustained cycling can be aerobic activity.
caution: A movement is not automatically moderate or vigorous for every person.

diagram.title: Aerobic exercise
diagram.caption: Brisk walking or sustained cycling can be aerobic activity.

name: Moderate intensity
definition: A level of aerobic effort that is meaningfully above easy activity. Relative intensity considers the person, while absolute intensity uses a standardized task measure.
example: In the talk test, you can talk but would have difficulty singing.
caution: A fixed walking speed may feel very different to two people.

diagram.title: Moderate intensity
diagram.caption: In the talk test, you can talk but would have difficulty singing.

name: Vigorous intensity
definition: A higher level of aerobic effort. In the talk test, speech is limited to a few words before pausing for breath.
example: A hard uphill effort may make full-sentence conversation difficult.
caution: Vigorous does not mean maximal, and symptoms should not be ignored to preserve a target.

diagram.title: Vigorous intensity
diagram.caption: A hard uphill effort may make full-sentence conversation difficult.

name: Talk test
definition: A practical method of estimating relative aerobic intensity from how comfortably you can speak during activity.
example: Comfortable conversation versus only a few words helps distinguish effort levels.
caution: It is a rough cue, not a direct lactate or ventilatory-threshold measurement.

diagram.title: Talk test
diagram.caption: Comfortable conversation versus only a few words helps distinguish effort levels.

name: Heart-rate zone
definition: A band of heart rates defined by a chosen model. Models may use maximum heart rate, heart-rate reserve, or measured thresholds.
example: Two apps can assign different zone boundaries to the same person.
caution: The label “zone 2” is incomplete without the system and settings behind it.

diagram.title: Heart-rate zone
diagram.caption: Two apps can assign different zone boundaries to the same person.

name: Heart-rate reserve
definition: The difference between maximum and resting heart rate. A reserve-based target adds a chosen fraction of that difference to resting heart rate.
example: If maximum is 180 and resting is 60 bpm, reserve is 120 bpm.
caution: Both input values can be uncertain. This example is arithmetic, not your training target.

diagram.title: Heart-rate reserve
diagram.caption: If maximum is 180 and resting is 60 bpm, reserve is 120 bpm.

name: Maximum heart rate
definition: The highest heart rate reached under appropriate maximal testing conditions. Age-based formulas predict population averages rather than a precise individual value.
example: A formula-generated maximum and a measured test maximum are different inputs.
caution: Do not treat an age formula as an exact safety boundary or self-test instruction.

diagram.title: Maximum heart rate
diagram.caption: A formula-generated maximum and a measured test maximum are different inputs.

name: MET
definition: Metabolic equivalent of task: a standardized expression of energy expenditure relative to a conventional resting reference.
example: An activity listed at 4 METs has a standardized intensity classification.
caution: MET tables are not individualized measurements of your calorie expenditure.

diagram.title: MET
diagram.caption: An activity listed at 4 METs has a standardized intensity classification.

name: VO2 max
definition: Maximum rate of oxygen uptake during an appropriate test, often expressed in mL/kg/min. Wearable values are estimates from algorithms.
example: A laboratory gas-analysis test and a watch estimate use different methods.
caution: Compare methods and conditions before interpreting a small change as adaptation.

diagram.title: VO2 max
diagram.caption: A laboratory gas-analysis test and a watch estimate use different methods.

name: Pace
definition: Time taken per unit of distance, such as minutes per kilometer. It is the inverse framing of speed.
example: 5:00 min/km corresponds to 12 km/h.
caution: A lower pace number means faster movement when distance units are unchanged.

diagram.title: Pace
diagram.caption: 5:00 min/km corresponds to 12 km/h.

name: Interval training
definition: Training that alternates defined work periods with recovery periods. Duration, intensity, repetitions, and recovery all define the session.
example: Six work bouts separated by easier movement form an interval structure.
caution: Intervals are not automatically maximal-effort sprints.

diagram.title: Interval training
diagram.caption: Six work bouts separated by easier movement form an interval structure.

name: Concurrent training
definition: A program that includes both aerobic and strength training over the same period. The arrangement and total demand affect practical results.
example: Two strength sessions plus two cycling sessions in a week is concurrent training.
caution: Combining modes does not automatically prevent strength or muscle gains.

diagram.title: Concurrent training
diagram.caption: Two strength sessions plus two cycling sessions in a week is concurrent training.

name: Interference effect
definition: A potential reduction in a specific adaptation when training demands are combined compared with a relevant single-mode program. It is outcome- and context-dependent.
example: Explosive performance may respond differently from muscle size in mixed programs.
caution: It is not a synonym for feeling tired after a run.

diagram.title: Interference effect
diagram.caption: Explosive performance may respond differently from muscle size in mixed programs.

name: Protein
definition: A macronutrient made from amino acids, used for structural and functional roles throughout the body, including muscle repair and adaptation.
example: Food sources include legumes, tofu, eggs, dairy, fish, and meat.
caution: More protein does not substitute for training, enough energy, or a varied diet.

diagram.title: Protein
diagram.caption: Food sources include legumes, tofu, eggs, dairy, fish, and meat.

name: Amino acid
definition: A building block of proteins. Essential amino acids must be obtained through the diet because the body cannot make enough to meet its needs.
example: Different protein foods supply different amino-acid patterns.
caution: A food’s protein content and its amino-acid profile are related but distinct properties.

diagram.title: Amino acid
diagram.caption: Different protein foods supply different amino-acid patterns.

name: Protein distribution
definition: How total daily protein is spread across eating occasions. It is separate from the total amount eaten.
example: 112 g could be distributed as four 28 g portions, but equal portions are not mandatory.
caution: Do not turn one idealized meal schedule into a requirement that makes ordinary eating difficult.

diagram.title: Protein distribution
diagram.caption: 112 g could be distributed as four 28 g portions, but equal portions are not mandatory.

name: Carbohydrate
definition: A broad nutrient category including sugars, starches, and fiber. Different carbohydrate foods also provide different mixtures of other nutrients.
example: Oats, beans, fruit, and rice all contribute carbohydrate.
caution: Carbohydrate amount alone does not describe a food’s overall quality.

diagram.title: Carbohydrate
diagram.caption: Oats, beans, fruit, and rice all contribute carbohydrate.

name: Glycogen
definition: A stored form of carbohydrate found mainly in muscle and liver. Its storage is associated with water, so changes can influence body mass.
example: A change in carbohydrate intake and training can alter glycogen and water storage.
caution: A rapid scale change is not automatically an equivalent change in fat tissue.

diagram.title: Glycogen
diagram.caption: A change in carbohydrate intake and training can alter glycogen and water storage.

name: Dietary fat
definition: A macronutrient that supplies energy and supports functions including absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Foods contain different fatty-acid mixtures.
example: Nuts, olive oil, avocado, and oily fish contribute dietary fat.
caution: Dietary fat and body-fat tissue are not interchangeable concepts.

diagram.title: Dietary fat
diagram.caption: Nuts, olive oil, avocado, and oily fish contribute dietary fat.

name: Macronutrient
definition: A nutrient category consumed in relatively large amounts. In common food tracking, macros refer to protein, carbohydrate, and fat.
example: A meal can be described by grams of protein, carbohydrate, and fat.
caution: A macro total does not describe all vitamins, minerals, fiber, or food quality.

diagram.title: Macronutrient
diagram.caption: A meal can be described by grams of protein, carbohydrate, and fat.

name: Micronutrient
definition: A vitamin or mineral needed in smaller quantities than macronutrients. Small required quantities do not imply small importance.
example: Iron, calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12 are micronutrients.
caution: More is not automatically better; some supplemental amounts can be harmful.

diagram.title: Micronutrient
diagram.caption: Iron, calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12 are micronutrients.

name: Fiber
definition: Dietary components, largely from plants, that resist digestion in the small intestine and can have varied physiological effects.
example: Beans, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables can contribute fiber.
caution: Different fibers have different properties; a single label number does not describe them all.

diagram.title: Fiber
diagram.caption: Beans, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables can contribute fiber.

name: Soluble fiber
definition: Fiber that dissolves or disperses in water. Some forms create viscous gels and some are fermented by gut microbes.
example: Oats and legumes contain soluble fiber alongside other components.
caution: Solubility, viscosity, and fermentability are separate properties, not synonyms.

diagram.title: Soluble fiber
diagram.caption: Oats and legumes contain soluble fiber alongside other components.

name: Insoluble fiber
definition: Fiber that does not dissolve readily in water. Many plant foods contain both soluble and insoluble fractions.
example: Whole grains and vegetables can supply insoluble fiber.
caution: The categories overlap in foods; they are not a reason to eat only one type.

diagram.title: Insoluble fiber
diagram.caption: Whole grains and vegetables can supply insoluble fiber.

name: Whole grain
definition: A grain retaining its bran, germ, and endosperm in their original relative proportions, whether intact or processed.
example: Oats and brown rice are familiar examples.
caution: A dark color or the word “multigrain” does not by itself prove a product is whole grain.

diagram.title: Whole grain
diagram.caption: Oats and brown rice are familiar examples.

name: Serving size
definition: The reference amount used to state nutrition information on a label. Its meaning depends on the labeling system.
example: A label may report nutrition per 30 g serving.
caution: It is not automatically the portion you ate or a personalized recommendation.

diagram.title: Serving size
diagram.caption: A label may report nutrition per 30 g serving.

name: Portion
definition: The amount of food you actually choose or consume on an occasion. It can differ from the label serving size.
example: A 45 g portion is 1.5 times a 30 g label serving.
caution: Record the actual amount before multiplying the label values.

diagram.title: Portion
diagram.caption: A 45 g portion is 1.5 times a 30 g label serving.

name: Percent Daily Value
definition: A U.S. label measure showing how a serving contributes to a reference daily nutrient amount. It supports general label comparisons.
example: A stated %DV applies to the serving shown on that label.
caution: Daily Values are reference amounts, not individual requirements, and other regions use different systems.

diagram.title: Percent Daily Value
diagram.caption: A stated %DV applies to the serving shown on that label.

name: Energy density
definition: The energy content per unit mass of food, often expressed as kcal per gram or per 100 grams.
example: 240 kcal per 100 g equals 2.4 kcal per gram.
caution: It does not alone describe nutrient quality, fullness, or an appropriate portion.

diagram.title: Energy density
diagram.caption: 240 kcal per 100 g equals 2.4 kcal per gram.

name: Calorie
definition: In food contexts, “calorie” usually means kilocalorie, abbreviated kcal. It is a unit of energy, not a type of nutrient.
example: 1 kcal equals 4.184 kilojoules.
caution: Check whether an app displays kcal or kJ before comparing values.

diagram.title: Calorie
diagram.caption: 1 kcal equals 4.184 kilojoules.

name: Energy balance
definition: The relationship between energy intake and energy expenditure over time. Changes in stored body energy are related to the difference.
example: A persistent imbalance can change energy stores, while daily scale readings also reflect water and contents.
caution: It is a dynamic relationship, not a perfect daily prediction from two app numbers.

diagram.title: Energy balance
diagram.caption: A persistent imbalance can change energy stores, while daily scale readings also reflect water and contents.

name: Calorie deficit
definition: A period in which energy intake is lower than energy expenditure. The size is usually estimated rather than directly measured in everyday life.
example: A planned intake below estimated maintenance is intended to create a deficit.
caution: A target in an app does not prove the actual deficit, and bigger is not automatically appropriate.

diagram.title: Calorie deficit
diagram.caption: A planned intake below estimated maintenance is intended to create a deficit.

name: Maintenance energy
definition: An estimated energy intake associated with stable body energy stores over a period under given conditions. It changes with circumstances.
example: A person’s maintenance estimate can differ after changes in body size or activity.
caution: It is not a fixed lifetime calorie number or a guarantee of identical daily scale readings.

diagram.title: Maintenance energy
diagram.caption: A person’s maintenance estimate can differ after changes in body size or activity.

name: Recipe yield
definition: The total amount or number of portions produced by a recipe. It determines how the recipe’s ingredient totals are divided.
example: A recipe containing 2,000 kcal divided into four equal portions gives about 500 kcal per portion.
caution: Equal portions by eye may not be equal by weight, and cooking changes water content.

diagram.title: Recipe yield
diagram.caption: A recipe containing 2,000 kcal divided into four equal portions gives about 500 kcal per portion.

name: Hydration
definition: The state of body water and fluid balance. It is influenced by intake, losses, and health circumstances rather than a single bottle count.
example: Water, other beverages, and water-containing foods all contribute to intake.
caution: A fixed daily target does not fit every climate, activity level, or medical situation.

diagram.title: Hydration
diagram.caption: Water, other beverages, and water-containing foods all contribute to intake.

name: Electrolyte
definition: A substance that forms electrically charged particles in solution. Sodium, potassium, and chloride are familiar examples relevant to body fluids.
example: Sweat contains water and electrolytes, including sodium.
caution: An electrolyte drink is not automatically necessary for every short workout.

diagram.title: Electrolyte
diagram.caption: Sweat contains water and electrolytes, including sodium.

name: Sodium
definition: A mineral and electrolyte involved in fluid balance and nerve and muscle function. Food labels often list sodium rather than total salt mass.
example: Sodium chloride is table salt; its sodium content is only part of its mass.
caution: Milligrams of sodium are not the same as milligrams of salt.

diagram.title: Sodium
diagram.caption: Sodium chloride is table salt; its sodium content is only part of its mass.

name: Sweat rate
definition: An estimate of sweat loss per unit time. Field estimates can use changes in body mass adjusted for fluid consumed and urine produced.
example: A session estimate is tied to its duration, environment, and activity.
caution: It does not automatically generalize to a different climate or intensity, and measurements contain error.

diagram.title: Sweat rate
diagram.caption: A session estimate is tied to its duration, environment, and activity.

name: Creatine
definition: A compound involved in rapid energy buffering through the creatine-phosphocreatine system. Creatine monohydrate is the best-studied supplemental form.
example: It is commonly studied with repeated high-intensity exercise and resistance training.
caution: It is not a stimulant and does not replace training or adequate food intake.

diagram.title: Creatine
diagram.caption: It is commonly studied with repeated high-intensity exercise and resistance training.

name: Phosphocreatine
definition: A phosphorylated form of creatine that can donate a phosphate to help regenerate ATP during demanding muscular work.
example: It contributes to rapid ATP replenishment during brief intense efforts.
caution: This energy system overlaps with others; it does not operate alone for an exact fixed number of seconds.

diagram.title: Phosphocreatine
diagram.caption: It contributes to rapid ATP replenishment during brief intense efforts.

name: Loading phase
definition: An initial period using a particular higher-intake protocol to increase a substance’s stores more quickly. In creatine use, loading is optional.
example: A creatine protocol may use loading before a lower maintenance intake.
caution: The term describes a protocol, not a requirement for everyone or permission to improvise large doses.

diagram.title: Loading phase
diagram.caption: A creatine protocol may use loading before a lower maintenance intake.

name: Supplement
definition: A product intended to supplement the diet. Ingredients, amounts, evidence, quality, and regulation differ between products and jurisdictions.
example: A protein powder or creatine product can be a supplement.
caution: A performance claim or high price does not establish safety, purity, or usefulness.

diagram.title: Supplement
diagram.caption: A protein powder or creatine product can be a supplement.

name: Caffeine
definition: A stimulant found in foods, drinks, medicines, and supplements. Response depends on dose, timing, sensitivity, and circumstances.
example: Coffee plus an energy drink contributes to the same day’s total intake.
caution: The FDA’s 400 mg adult reference is not a recommended target or a guarantee for everyone.

diagram.title: Caffeine
diagram.caption: Coffee plus an energy drink contributes to the same day’s total intake.

name: Recovery
definition: The processes and time associated with restoring capacity after training and other demands. Different tissues and performance measures can recover at different rates.
example: You may feel less sore before a particular performance measure returns to its usual level.
caution: No single score captures every aspect of recovery.

diagram.title: Recovery
diagram.caption: You may feel less sore before a particular performance measure returns to its usual level.

name: Fatigue
definition: A reduction in the ability or willingness to perform a task, with multiple possible physical and psychological contributors. It is not one diagnosis.
example: A usual load may feel harder after a demanding week.
caution: A difficult set does not identify the cause. Consider sleep, illness, schedule, and the task itself.

diagram.title: Fatigue
diagram.caption: A usual load may feel harder after a demanding week.

name: Deload
definition: A planned reduction in training demand for a defined period. Programs implement it in different ways.
example: You reduce working-set count for a busy week and review before rebuilding.
caution: There is no universal percentage or calendar that every trainee needs.

diagram.title: Deload
diagram.caption: You reduce working-set count for a busy week and review before rebuilding.

name: DOMS
definition: Delayed-onset muscle soreness: discomfort developing after exercise, often after unfamiliar or demanding work. It is not a direct measure of adaptation.
example: You notice thigh soreness the day after a new exercise variation.
caution: Sharp pain, severe weakness, or unusual symptoms should not automatically be labeled ordinary soreness.

diagram.title: DOMS
diagram.caption: You notice thigh soreness the day after a new exercise variation.

name: Sleep opportunity
definition: The amount of time made available for sleep, such as the interval between going to bed and getting up. It is not all necessarily spent asleep.
example: 23:00 to 07:00 provides an eight-hour opportunity.
caution: Awake periods reduce actual sleep time even when the schedule looks adequate.

diagram.title: Sleep opportunity
diagram.caption: 23:00 to 07:00 provides an eight-hour opportunity.

name: Sleep duration
definition: The amount of time actually spent asleep during a defined period. Self-reports and wearables estimate it in different ways.
example: Eight hours in bed with awake periods can mean less than eight hours of sleep.
caution: Do not treat time in bed or a device estimate as a perfectly measured duration.

diagram.title: Sleep duration
diagram.caption: Eight hours in bed with awake periods can mean less than eight hours of sleep.

name: Sleep efficiency
definition: The proportion of time in bed spent asleep, usually expressed as a percentage. It depends on how both times are measured.
example: Seven hours asleep during eight hours in bed gives 87.5%.
caution: A high percentage can coexist with too little total sleep opportunity.

diagram.title: Sleep efficiency
diagram.caption: Seven hours asleep during eight hours in bed gives 87.5%.

name: Circadian rhythm
definition: An approximately 24-hour biological rhythm involved in timing many body processes, including the sleep-wake pattern.
example: Light exposure and habitual timing can influence sleep scheduling.
caution: It is not the same as the amount of sleep pressure accumulated while awake.

diagram.title: Circadian rhythm
diagram.caption: Light exposure and habitual timing can influence sleep scheduling.

name: Cool-down
definition: A period of gradually reduced activity after the main session, allowing a more gradual transition toward rest.
example: After aerobic work, you continue at an easier pace before stopping.
caution: It is not a guarantee against soreness or an excuse to force painful stretching.

diagram.title: Cool-down
diagram.caption: After aerobic work, you continue at an easier pace before stopping.

name: Mobility
definition: A practical term for the ability to access and control movement through a range. It is used differently across coaching settings.
example: You practice controlled movement through the range needed for a particular exercise.
caution: It is broader than a single flexibility measurement, and more range is not automatically better for every task.

diagram.title: Mobility
diagram.caption: You practice controlled movement through the range needed for a particular exercise.

name: Training log
definition: A record of the work performed and the context needed to interpret it. Its usefulness depends on consistency and accurate units.
example: An exercise entry includes load, repetitions, effort, and relevant setup notes.
caution: A long record with inconsistent conventions can be less useful than a short, repeatable one.

diagram.title: Training log
diagram.caption: An exercise entry includes load, repetitions, effort, and relevant setup notes.

name: Personal record
definition: Your best recorded performance on a defined task and standard. The task definition should remain visible.
example: A best set of ten at a fixed movement standard is a rep-specific record.
caution: Changing equipment, range, or counting conventions can create an apparent record without a fair comparison.

diagram.title: Personal record
diagram.caption: A best set of ten at a fixed movement standard is a rep-specific record.

name: Baseline
definition: A reference set of observations used for comparison. A useful baseline represents the measurement conditions and period you intend to compare against.
example: Several comparable morning measurements form a more informative reference than one unusual day.
caution: A baseline is a reference, not a permanent personal norm.

diagram.title: Baseline
diagram.caption: Several comparable morning measurements form a more informative reference than one unusual day.

name: Trend
definition: A pattern of change across multiple observations. Its interpretation depends on noise, missing data, and how the values were collected.
example: Several weeks of consistent records can show a pattern that one day cannot.
caution: A trend line does not establish why the change happened.

diagram.title: Trend
diagram.caption: Several weeks of consistent records can show a pattern that one day cannot.

name: Rolling average
definition: An average recalculated over a moving window of observations. It smooths short-term variation while lagging some changes.
example: A seven-day average updates as a new day enters and an old day leaves the window.
caution: Missing values and the choice of window can change the result. State the method.

diagram.title: Rolling average
diagram.caption: A seven-day average updates as a new day enters and an old day leaves the window.

name: Missing data
definition: An observation that was not recorded or is unavailable. Its absence is different from a measured zero.
example: A day without a step record is not necessarily a day with zero steps.
caution: Silently replacing missing values with zero can distort totals and averages.

diagram.title: Missing data
diagram.caption: A day without a step record is not necessarily a day with zero steps.

name: Measurement error
definition: The difference or uncertainty introduced by a measurement process. It can include systematic bias and random variation.
example: Device fit or a changed scale position can affect recorded values.
caution: A small difference may reflect the method rather than a meaningful change in the person.

diagram.title: Measurement error
diagram.caption: Device fit or a changed scale position can affect recorded values.

name: Body mass
definition: The mass measured by a scale, including body tissues, water, and contents. It is not a direct measurement of body fat.
example: Food, fluid, and glycogen-related changes can affect short-term readings.
caution: Do not interpret each daily change as fat gained or lost.

diagram.title: Body mass
diagram.caption: Food, fluid, and glycogen-related changes can affect short-term readings.

name: Resting heart rate
definition: Heart rate measured or estimated under resting conditions. Devices may define the daily resting value differently.
example: A watch-derived resting value may use a different time window from a seated manual measurement.
caution: Compare methods and circumstances before interpreting small changes.

diagram.title: Resting heart rate
diagram.caption: A watch-derived resting value may use a different time window from a seated manual measurement.

name: HRV
definition: Heart-rate variability: variation in intervals between consecutive heartbeats. Different HRV statistics describe different features and use different units.
example: A device may report an RMSSD-based value in milliseconds.
caution: It is not the same as heart rate, and higher is not universally better. Do not compare unlike metrics or devices casually.

diagram.title: HRV
diagram.caption: A device may report an RMSSD-based value in milliseconds.

name: Readiness score
definition: A device- or app-specific composite estimate intended to summarize factors related to readiness. Inputs and weighting vary.
example: A score may combine recent sleep, activity, and heart-rate information.
caution: It is not a diagnosis or a universally comparable measurement across brands.

diagram.title: Readiness score
diagram.caption: A score may combine recent sleep, activity, and heart-rate information.

name: Correlation
definition: A statistical description of how variables vary together. It does not by itself establish that one caused the other.
example: Your better sessions may occur on days with more sleep, but other factors may also differ.
caution: A small personal dataset can show patterns by chance or through confounding factors.

diagram.title: Correlation
diagram.caption: Your better sessions may occur on days with more sleep, but other factors may also differ.
